transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, Dr. [Name]. Thank you for fitting me in. Well, I came in today because... gosh, where do I even start? I just seem to worry about absolutely everything now. And I mean everything. 

I’m a real estate broker, and, you know, you always have a little stress with the job, but lately my worry about my clients and the housing market—which, granted, is a bit all over the place right now with the rates—but my reaction to it just feels completely out of proportion to what is actually happening. I know the business, I’ve been doing this a long time, but I just can't stop fretting over every little detail. 

And it’s not just work, it spills over into everything else. I worry about my family constantly, I worry about money even though we're okay, it's... oh, even this condo! We recently moved to a condo, downsizing, you know, which was supposed to make life simpler, but I just agonize over whether it was the right decision. I'll sit there and think, 'Did we make a mistake? What if it doesn't appreciate? Did we sell the house at the wrong time?' It’s just exhausting. I know it’s too much, I know I shouldn't be this wound up over things that are mostly fine, but my brain just won't let it go and I just don't know how to turn it off anymore.
Have you noticed any recurring thoughts that you can’t seem to get out of your head, or do you find yourself doing certain things over and over again to try to reduce your anxiety?

No, not exactly. I mean, I don't have one specific thought that just loops like a broken record, and I certainly don't do things over and over again to make it stop. I know some people have to, you know, check the locks a dozen times or wash their hands constantly, but it’s nothing like that for me. It’s not a specific action I have to perform. 

Although, I suppose my husband would say I check my phone for work emails too much, but honestly, in real estate, especially right now, if you miss a text from a buyer's agent, you could lose the whole deal, so that's just being responsible. That's just the job. But as for the thoughts... it's not one single recurring thought, it's more like a domino effect. It just travels from one thing to the next. 

Like with the condo, I'll start out wondering if we got a good interest rate on the mortgage, and then suddenly I'm worrying about the building's HOA reserves, and then that makes me worry about our own personal retirement accounts, and then I'm stressing over whether my daughter is saving enough in her 401k... it just spirals. It’s never just one thought stuck in my head, it's a whole parade of different worries. And I don't do anything to try and reduce it because, well, I don't even know what I *could* do to stop it. It just keeps flowing from one topic to another all day long, completely on its own.
Have you noticed any physical symptoms like restlessness, trouble sleeping, muscle tension, or irritability that seem to go along with all this worrying?

Well, yes, actually. The sleeping part is... it's just awful. You know, I try to do everything right. I make sure I'm in bed at a reasonable hour, usually by 10:30 or 11:00, because I know how important rest is, especially at my age, and especially when you have to be "on" for clients all day. But getting into bed and actually sleeping are two very different things for me lately. 

I’ll lay there, and it’s like my brain just clicks into overdrive the second the lights go out. I’ll start thinking about the condo fees—because they just raised them again, and I wonder if they're going to keep going up and if we should have factored that in more—and then my mind jumps to the showings I have the next day. I'll start mentally walking through the properties, wondering if the staging is right, if I should have brought fresh flowers for the kitchen island, if I missed some tiny clause in a contract I sent over for signatures earlier that afternoon... 

It just circles and circles, and I'm lying there staring at the ceiling for what feels like hours. It takes me so long to finally settle down and drift off. And even when I do finally fall asleep, I don't think it's good sleep, you know? Because when my alarm goes off, I wake up feeling completely drained, like I never fully rested at all. I drag myself out of bed feeling just as exhausted as when I got in it. It’s like my brain is running a marathon while I’m supposed to be recharging. So yes, the sleep is definitely a big problem.
How long have you been feeling this way, with constant worrying and trouble sleeping?

Well, let me think... it's been quite a while now. I'd say it really started about a year and two months ago. Yes, right around then. That's when we finally sold our house—the one we'd lived in for over thirty years, where we raised our daughter, you know? It was a beautiful place, a big colonial, but it was just getting to be too much upkeep for the two of us, especially with my husband's knees acting up, and the yard work was endless. 

So we decided to downsize and move into this condo. Which, at the time, seemed like the most sensible thing in the world. We found a lovely unit, great natural light, close to downtown... but almost the minute the ink was dry on the closing papers, this whole... cloud of worry just descended on me. 

I remember the first few nights in the new place, surrounded by all those boxes. I should have been relieved that the move was over, but instead, I was just lying awake, staring at an unfamiliar ceiling, second-guessing everything. Did we get enough for the house? Did we overpay for the condo? Are the neighbors going to be noisy? What if the building has structural issues they didn't disclose? And it just never stopped. It started with the move, about fourteen months ago, and instead of settling down once we got unpacked, the worrying just sort of... expanded. It latched onto the move first, and then it just kept finding new things to attach itself to, right up until today.
Have you had any days where you felt down, hopeless, or lost interest in things you usually enjoy, for most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks at a time?

Well, no, not really. I mean, I wouldn't say I feel hopeless or down in the dumps like that. It's not a sadness, if that makes sense. It's more of a... a constant buzzing energy, but not the good kind of energy. It's that nervous, on-edge feeling, like I'm waiting for the other shoe to drop all the time. 

I certainly haven't lost interest in things. I still love my job, even though the market is just completely unpredictable right now—one minute houses are sitting for sixty days, and the next, there's a bidding war on a complete fixer-upper. I still enjoy taking my clients out, showing them properties, negotiating the deals. In fact, sometimes I think I throw myself into the work *too* much because it gives my brain something specific to focus on, even if I end up worrying about the contracts later. 

And I still love seeing my daughter, of course, and going out to dinner with my husband. We have this little Italian place we go to every Friday night, and I still look forward to that. We've been going there for fifteen years, they know exactly how I like my chicken piccata... So, no, I haven't lost interest in my life or felt hopeless for weeks on end. It’s just that I can’t seem to enjoy any of those things fully because there's always this underlying current of worry running through my mind while I'm doing them. I'm sitting there at dinner, eating my chicken, and part of my brain is wondering if I remembered to lock the patio door at the condo, or if the HOA is going to send out another special assessment notice. But no, no deep depression or hopelessness like you're describing. Just the worrying.
Do you find that you feel anxious or worried most days, even when there isn’t a specific problem or stressor happening at that moment?

Well, yes. Yes, I do. That's exactly why I'm here, actually, because it feels like I worry about absolutely everything now, even when I'm just sitting on the sofa and nothing is technically wrong. It's just constant. I'll be sitting there, and suddenly I'm worrying about my clients, you know? Did I price that new listing correctly? Should we have painted the trim before putting it on the market? And then that spirals into worrying about the real estate market in general, because interest rates are doing whatever they're doing, and who knows if buyers are going to dry up completely by spring. 

And then, if it's not work, it's my family. I worry about my daughter, even though she's thirty-two and perfectly capable, but I'll wonder if she's saving enough for retirement or if she's working too many hours. And money—oh, I worry about money constantly, even though we made a good profit on the house. I just sit there and think, what if inflation eats away at our savings? What if my husband's knees get worse and he needs surgery and Medicare doesn't cover all the physical therapy? 

And of course, there's the condo. I'm still second-guessing if moving was the right decision, even on a quiet Sunday morning when nothing is happening. I'll just be drinking my coffee, and my mind is racing through all these scenarios, and... and I know, logically, that it's out of proportion. I know I'm making mountains out of molehills, but I just can't seem to stop the wheels from turning. It's like my brain is always searching for a problem to solve, even when there isn't one right in front of me.
Do you often feel fatigued or low on energy, even when you haven’t been doing anything particularly taxing?

Fatigued? You know, it's funny you ask that, because my husband, Richard, was just saying the other day that he doesn't know how I keep going at the pace I do. So, no, I wouldn't say I feel fatigued or low on energy at all. If anything, it's the exact opposite. Like I was saying before about that buzzing feeling? It's like I have too much energy, but it's all just... nervous energy. 

I'll be up at six in the morning, making coffee, pulling up the MLS listings on my iPad to see what went active overnight or what had a price drop, and from there I'm just... go, go, go. I'll run over to the condo association meeting—because let me tell you, if you don't stay on top of those people, they'll pass a special assessment for landscaping before you can even blink—and then I'm off showing houses all afternoon. 

But even when I haven't done anything taxing, like if I actually try to just sit down on a Sunday afternoon and watch a movie with Richard or read a book... I can't just sit there. My body might be resting, but my mind is running an absolute marathon, and I just end up getting up and reorganizing the hall closet or drafting emails to my clients for Monday morning. I'm just constantly revved up. Honestly, sometimes I wish I *could* feel a little fatigued, just so I could finally sit still for five minutes without feeling like I need to be doing something or checking on something. So, no, definitely no lack of energy here. Just the opposite, really.
Have you noticed any trouble focusing or concentrating, like your mind going blank or being unable to stay on task because of all the worrying?

Well, yes, actually. That is something I’ve really been noticing lately, and it’s incredibly frustrating because, in my line of work, you absolutely cannot afford to miss a detail. Real estate is all about the details—the dates, the contingencies, the disclosures. But lately, with all this constant worrying I was telling you about, it’s like my brain just gets hijacked. 

For instance, just the other day I was sitting at my desk—well, my new desk at the condo, which I’m still trying to get organized because the lighting in that room is completely different from my old office—and I was trying to review a purchase agreement for my clients, the Millers. They’re buying this lovely mid-century modern place, but the inspection came back with some issues on the HVAC system, so I was drafting the inspection addendum. And I swear to you, I sat there and read the exact same paragraph three or four times. I’d start reading, and then suddenly I’m thinking, "Did I schedule the termite inspector for Tuesday or Wednesday?" or "What if the sellers completely reject this addendum and the whole deal falls apart and the Millers lose their earnest money?" 

And before I know it, I’m at the bottom of the page and I have absolutely no idea what I just read. My mind just goes completely blank on the task at hand because this other worry just barges in and takes over. I lose the thread entirely. I have to physically stop, take a breath, and force myself back to the top of the page. It’s exhausting, to be honest. I’ve always prided myself on being sharp and catching every little thing in these contracts, but now it takes me twice as long to get through a simple document because I just can't keep my focus where it needs to be. The worry just pulls me right out of it.
Have you ever experienced sudden episodes of intense fear or discomfort, where you felt like your heart was racing, you couldn't breathe, or you were losing control?

No, I can't say I've ever had anything quite like that. Sudden episodes of intense fear? No, it's not like that at all. It's not a sudden spike or a panic, you know, where I feel like I'm losing control or can't breathe. I've heard of people having those—my sister-in-law, actually, had a terrible time with them after her divorce, said she felt like she was having a heart attack right in the middle of the grocery store by the produce section. But for me, it's never been like that. 

My heart doesn't suddenly start pounding out of my chest, and I don't get that suffocating feeling. It's more of a... well, like I was saying before, it's a constant, low-level hum of worry. It's always there, always churning in the background. It's not a sudden attack that comes out of nowhere and knocks me off my feet; it's just this steady stream of "what ifs" that I can't seem to turn off. Like, I'll be driving to a showing, and instead of just listening to the radio, I'm running through every possible thing that could go wrong with the appraisal, or wondering if I remembered to lock the back door at the condo, or worrying if Richard remembered to take his blood pressure medication. 

So, no, I wouldn't describe it as sudden or intense fear. I'm always very much in control, maybe too in control, honestly, because I'm trying to manage all these potential disasters in my head before they even happen. It's just exhausting because it never really peaks and goes away; it just stays with me all day long. But no, no racing heart or feeling like I can't breathe or anything like that. Just the constant, never-ending worry.
Have you noticed yourself becoming more irritable or easily annoyed, especially when you're feeling overwhelmed by all the worrying?

Irritable? Oh, well... I mean, I suppose Richard might say so, but I don't really think I'm any more irritable than anyone else would be in my shoes. I mean, if you want to talk about being easily annoyed, you have to look at what I'm dealing with on a daily basis. 

Just yesterday, for example, I was trying to coordinate a final walk-through for a property over on Elm Street—a beautiful colonial, completely updated kitchen, but the sellers are just dragging their feet on moving their things out. And I'm sitting there, my mind is already spinning about whether the title company has the updated payoff statement, and whether the buyer's lender is going to clear the file to close on time, and then my phone rings. And it's the listing agent, telling me they need another day to get the garage cleaned out. 

Well, I just... I completely snapped at him. I told him that a contract is a contract and they can't just change the terms at the eleventh hour because they didn't plan their packing properly. And after I hung up, I did feel a little bad, because usually I'm very professional, very diplomatic. But it's like, when my brain is already juggling fifteen different "what ifs" and I'm so worried about everything falling apart, my patience is just... it's just nonexistent. 

And it happens with Richard, too, bless his heart. He'll ask me something simple, like what we should have for dinner, while I'm in the middle of worrying about an inspection report, and I'll just bite his head off. I'll say, "I can't possibly think about chicken versus fish right now, Richard, the entire plumbing system at the Oakwood house might need to be replaced!" So... I guess, yes, maybe I am a bit more irritable lately. But it's not like I'm just walking around angry for no reason. It's just that when I'm so overwhelmed by all the things that could go wrong, any little interruption or extra problem just feels like the straw that breaks the camel's back, you know? I just don't have the bandwidth for it.
Do you ever notice symptoms like a fast heartbeat, sweating, trembling, or feeling shaky when your anxiety gets particularly intense?

Sweating or trembling? No, not really. It’s kind of like what we were talking about earlier with the sudden panic—I just don't get those physical reactions. I mean, my mind will be going a million miles a minute, but my body doesn't really do all of that shaking or sweating. 

I actually had the perfect scenario for that just last Sunday, over in the Heritage subdivision. I was hosting an open house for this gorgeous four-bedroom craftsman. The sellers, lovely people, but they have three golden retrievers, so I had spent the entire morning just making sure there wasn't a single dog hair in sight, spraying linen mist, getting the lighting just right. And literally ten minutes before the open house is supposed to start, I realize the air conditioning isn't kicking on. It’s the middle of the afternoon, the sun is beating down on the big bay windows, and the thermostat is just climbing. 

Now, my mind immediately started spiraling. I’m thinking, "The buyers are going to walk in, they’re going to feel the heat, they’re going to assume the HVAC is completely shot, they’re going to think the house is a money pit, and this listing is going to sit on the market for months." I was worrying about having to explain to the sellers why we didn't get any offers, worrying about whether I should try to call an emergency repairman on a Sunday, which costs an absolute fortune. 

But even with all of that intense worry just flooding my brain, I wasn't physically shaking. My hands weren't trembling when I was setting out the sign-in sheets, and my heart wasn't racing. I mean, I might have been a little warm because the house was literally heating up, but I wasn't in a cold sweat or having nervous palpitations or anything like that. I was perfectly steady on the outside, greeting people at the door with a smile, handing out brochures. You would never look at me and think, "Oh, she's trembling," or "She looks shaky." It’s all entirely internal. It’s just that relentless mental churning, not my body actually shaking or my heart pounding out of my chest. So, no, I haven't really noticed any of those physical things you mentioned.
Do you feel like you have a hard time controlling your worrying, even when you know it's not rational or necessary?

Oh, absolutely. It’s... it’s exactly like that. It’s like a runaway train, honestly. I know in my logical brain—I have a degree, I’ve been in this business for decades, I know how these transactions work—I know that most of what I’m worrying about isn’t going to happen, or at least, it’s not life-or-death. But stopping it? That’s an entirely different story. 

Just the other night, for instance, it was maybe 9:30 or 10:00, Richard was already asleep, and I was just doing a quick check of my emails on my iPad before turning out the light. And there was a message from a buyer's agent on a beautiful little townhome I have listed over in the new development on Pine Street. Just a simple question, really, asking if the seller would be willing to leave the custom drapes in the dining room. Now, normally, that’s a five-minute conversation for the next business day. No big deal. 

I literally said out loud to the empty room, I said, "Parin, this is not urgent." I told myself to just put it away. I closed the iPad, I turned off the lamp, and I laid my head on the pillow. But then I’m lying there in the dark, and my brain just starts going. I start thinking, well, if they want the drapes, maybe they’re going to be nitpicky about the inspection items. And if they’re difficult about the inspection, what if they ask for a credit for that tiny, old water stain in the guest bath? And if they ask for a credit, my sellers might get offended and want to kill the deal. And suddenly, I’m worrying about the house going back on the market, and the days on market ticking up, and having to explain to the sellers why we lost the buyer... 

It’s just... one concern leads to another, you know? It's a complete domino effect in my head. And before I know it, I’ve spent half an hour just lying there replaying small details I meant to let go of. I’ll go over every single word in that short email, wondering if the agent's tone was aggressive, or if I should have just negotiated the drapes in the initial contract. It’s completely irrational, I know it is! I know I need to sleep. But I just can't seem to put the brakes on it once it starts. I just can't turn the worry off.
Have you ever felt fatigued or experienced a loss of energy for no clear reason, even when you haven’t been doing much?

Fatigued for no reason? Oh, heavens, no. No, if anything, I think I have the exact opposite problem. I mean, my mind is always going so fast that it just pulls my body right along with it. If I'm tired, there is always a very, very clear reason for it. I certainly don't just sit around feeling drained out of nowhere. 

Just to give you an idea of what my schedule is like, let me tell you about my Thursday. I was up at 5:30 in the morning because I had to meet a staging company at this gorgeous mid-century modern over on Maple Drive—prime location, absolutely stunning original hardwood floors, but the sellers had completely moved out, so it was just an empty box. And I get there, and the stagers are unloading the truck, and I realize they’ve brought this dreadful, cool-toned gray sectional for the living room, which completely clashed with the warm teak paneling on the accent wall. I mean, it was a disaster waiting to happen. Buyers are so visual, they would have walked in and just felt like the room was cold, you know? 

So, I spent the next three hours personally driving back and forth to their warehouse across town to help them pick out a beautiful cognac leather sofa instead. And then I had two back-to-back showings in the afternoon, plus a final walk-through where the buyer threw an absolute fit because a lightbulb was burnt out in the half-bath—which I ended up changing myself, by the way, in a pencil skirt and heels—and then I didn't get home to Richard until almost 8:00 PM. 

So, when I finally sat down on the couch and felt tired, well, I had certainly earned it! It wasn't just some mysterious loss of energy. I was exhausted because I had been running on pure adrenaline and espresso for fourteen hours straight. So, no, I really can't say I ever just feel fatigued for no reason. I’m always on the go, always doing something, and honestly, even when I *want* to feel tired and just relax, my brain is usually still buzzing too much to let me.
Do you often have trouble falling asleep or staying asleep, even when you’re not actively thinking about something specific?

Well, see, that's the trick of it—I am almost *always* actively thinking about something specific. I really do try my best to have good habits. Most nights I get into bed at a perfectly reasonable hour, usually right after I put the iPad away like I mentioned earlier. I want to be asleep by ten because my mornings are just so demanding in this business. 

But my mind just refuses to cooperate. It just keeps circling and circling through all the minutiae of the day. I’ll be lying there in the quiet, and suddenly I’m going over condo fees for a new listing, trying to remember if the special assessment for the roof was already paid out by the seller or if the buyer has to assume it. And then, before I know it, I’m mentally mapping out tomorrow’s showings, worrying if I left enough buffer time for traffic between the west side properties and the suburbs. And then I'll start second-guessing myself, just agonizing over whether I missed something in a contract I submitted that afternoon—did I check the right box for the appraisal contingency? Did I get all the required initials on the lead paint disclosure? 

It takes me such a terribly long time to finally settle down and drift off because I'm just reviewing all these files in my head, over and over. And because of all that mental gymnastics, when the alarm finally does go off, I wake up feeling like I never fully rested at all. It's like my brain was working the night shift while I was supposed to be sleeping, so I just start the next day feeling completely unrefreshed.
Have you ever found yourself excessively worried about your physical health or specific bodily symptoms, even when doctors have told you there’s no serious issue?

Oh, no, not at all. My health is probably the one thing I *don't* obsess over. Honestly, I just don't have the time to sit around wondering about every little ache and pain! If something hurts, I usually know exactly why it hurts, and it's almost always related to my schedule. 

Like, just last month, I had this terrible, shooting pain in my lower back, just radiating down my left leg. Richard was practically hovering over me, telling me I needed to go to a specialist, worrying it could be a slipped disc or some kind of permanent nerve damage or something awful. But I told him, I said, "Richard, I have been walking up and down three flights of stairs at those new luxury builds on Elm Street for three days straight, and I’ve been doing it in two-inch heels because the developer was on-site and I needed to look sharp." I didn't think for a second it was some mysterious, life-threatening disease. I just knew it was the stairs and the shoes!

I did end up going to my regular doctor, Dr. Aris, mostly just to get Richard to stop nagging me about it. And Dr. Aris did a quick exam and said it was just a bit of mild sciatica from overuse, told me to take some ibuprofen and maybe switch to flats for a few days. Which, by the way, is practically impossible in high-end real estate if you want to maintain a certain level of professionalism, but I digress. 

The point is, when he told me it was nothing serious, I completely believed him. I was just relieved I didn't have to take time off! I didn't go home and look up symptoms on the internet or demand an MRI or worry that he missed something. I just went to the department store, bought a pair of sensible wedges with decent arch support, and went right back to work. So, no, I don't really worry about my body failing me or anything like that. It’s the escrows and the appraisals that give me gray hair, not my health!
Do you ever feel particularly anxious or distressed when you're away from family members or worried about something bad happening to them when you're not around?

Oh, no, not really. I mean, Richard and I have been married for thirty-four years, and our daughter, Chloe, she's thirty-two now and lives in Chicago, so we're all very independent people. I certainly don't sit around worrying that something terrible is going to happen to them just because I'm not in the room. 

In fact, just last week, Richard went on this fishing trip with his brother up to a lake in Michigan. They go every year, and they are completely off the grid for four days. No cell service, no Wi-Fi, nothing. And honestly, it is wonderful! I don't mean that in a bad way, of course I love him, but having the house to myself for a few days? It's glorious. I can spread out all my listing paperwork on the dining room table without him complaining about the mess, I can watch my home renovation shows on HGTV without him making sarcastic comments about the open-concept floor plans, and I can just focus entirely on my clients. 

I didn't spend one single second of those four days worrying that his boat had capsized or that he'd been eaten by a bear or whatever else could happen in the woods. I knew he was with his brother, they know what they're doing, and I had three open houses to prep for that weekend anyway. I was far more concerned about whether the caterer was going to deliver the artisan cheese platters on time for the Sunday showing at the new subdivision than I was about Richard's fishing trip. 

And it's the same with Chloe. She travels all the time for her consulting job—she's always flying off to Denver or Seattle or New York. And she's a smart girl, she knows how to handle herself in an airport and navigate a new city. I don't feel the need to track her flights or text her every five minutes to make sure she made it to her hotel safely. We'll catch up on Sunday evenings, she'll tell me about her week, I'll tell her about the absolute nightmare I had trying to negotiate a seller down on a property that needed a new HVAC system, and that's that. So, no, I don't have that kind of anxiety about being apart from my family at all. My worries are almost entirely reserved for my real estate transactions, I assure you!
Do you find that your worries are often focused on your work performance or responsibilities, even when there’s no immediate problem?

Well, yes, work is a huge part of it, like I was just saying about the contracts and the escrows. But honestly, doctor, that's exactly why I finally made this appointment. It’s not just work anymore. I came in because I seem to worry about absolutely everything now. I mean, it just never stops. 

Yes, it’s my clients, and it’s the housing market—which, with the way interest rates are fluctuating right now, you can imagine the stress, it's enough to give anyone an ulcer—but it bleeds into everything else. It's money, it's my family... and I know I just said I don't panic when Richard goes off the grid or when Chloe travels, but I do worry about them in other ways, constantly. Are they saving enough for retirement? Is Chloe working too many hours? 

And then there are these big life choices that just consume my thoughts. Like, we recently downsized, and I spend hours just agonizing over whether moving to the condo was the right decision. I'll sit there at the kitchen island, looking at the quartz countertops, and just fret about whether we rushed into it, or if the HOA board is going to mismanage the reserve funds, or if we should have kept the larger house just in case. 

And the frustrating thing is, I know it doesn't make sense. I step back and look at all of this—the clients, the market, the family, the money, the condo—and it just feels completely out of proportion to what is actually happening. There's almost never an immediate problem! The condo is lovely, the market always ebbs and flows, everyone is fine... but my brain just treats every single little thing like an absolute crisis, and I just can't seem to turn the volume down on it.

candidates: F32 Major Depressive Disorder, Single Episode
inference_history.note: The patient presents with excessive worry across multiple domains, including work, family, financial decisions, and life changes (e.g., moving to a condo). The concern about decisions and future outcomes, and the description of being 'completely out of proportion' to the actual situation, raises initial suspicion for Generalized Anxiety Disorder (F41.1). Other anxiety-related disorders (e.g., adjustment disorder, OCD, social anxiety) and depression remain in the differential at this early stage. No definitive exclusions are made yet.

Patient describes a 'domino effect' of worry across multiple domains without ritualistic coping behaviors, making OCD less likely. patient.answer:
Hi, Dr. [Name]. Thank you for fitting me in. Well, I came in today because... gosh, where do I even start? I just seem to worry about absolutely everything now. And I mean everything. 

I’m a real estate broker, and, you know, you always have a little stress with the job, but lately my worry about my clients and the housing market—which, granted, is a bit all over the place right now with the rates—but my reaction to it just feels completely out of proportion to what is actually happening. I know the business, I’ve been doing this a long time, but I just can't stop fretting over every little detail. 

And it’s not just work, it spills over into everything else. I worry about my family constantly, I worry about money even though we're okay, it's... oh, even this condo! We recently moved to a condo, downsizing, you know, which was supposed to make life simpler, but I just agonize over whether it was the right decision. I'll sit there and think, 'Did we make a mistake? What if it doesn't appreciate? Did we sell the house at the wrong time?' It’s just exhausting. I know it’s too much, I know I shouldn't be this wound up over things that are mostly fine, but my brain just won't let it go and I just don't know how to turn it off anymore.

patient.answer:
No, not exactly. I mean, I don't have one specific thought that just loops like a broken record, and I certainly don't do things over and over again to make it stop. I know some people have to, you know, check the locks a dozen times or wash their hands constantly, but it’s nothing like that for me. It’s not a specific action I have to perform. 

Although, I suppose my husband would say I check my phone for work emails too much, but honestly, in real estate, especially right now, if you miss a text from a buyer's agent, you could lose the whole deal, so that's just being responsible. That's just the job. But as for the thoughts... it's not one single recurring thought, it's more like a domino effect. It just travels from one thing to the next. 

Like with the condo, I'll start out wondering if we got a good interest rate on the mortgage, and then suddenly I'm worrying about the building's HOA reserves, and then that makes me worry about our own personal retirement accounts, and then I'm stressing over whether my daughter is saving enough in her 401k... it just spirals. It’s never just one thought stuck in my head, it's a whole parade of different worries. And I don't do anything to try and reduce it because, well, I don't even know what I *could* do to stop it. It just keeps flowing from one topic to another all day long, completely on its own.

patient.answer:
Well, yes, actually. The sleeping part is... it's just awful. You know, I try to do everything right. I make sure I'm in bed at a reasonable hour, usually by 10:30 or 11:00, because I know how important rest is, especially at my age, and especially when you have to be "on" for clients all day. But getting into bed and actually sleeping are two very different things for me lately. 

I’ll lay there, and it’s like my brain just clicks into overdrive the second the lights go out. I’ll start thinking about the condo fees—because they just raised them again, and I wonder if they're going to keep going up and if we should have factored that in more—and then my mind jumps to the showings I have the next day. I'll start mentally walking through the properties, wondering if the staging is right, if I should have brought fresh flowers for the kitchen island, if I missed some tiny clause in a contract I sent over for signatures earlier that afternoon... 

It just circles and circles, and I'm lying there staring at the ceiling for what feels like hours. It takes me so long to finally settle down and drift off. And even when I do finally fall asleep, I don't think it's good sleep, you know? Because when my alarm goes off, I wake up feeling completely drained, like I never fully rested at all. I drag myself out of bed feeling just as exhausted as when I got in it. It’s like my brain is running a marathon while I’m supposed to be recharging. So yes, the sleep is definitely a big problem.

doctor.intent: Assess the duration of the patient's symptoms to differentiate between adjustment disorder and generalized anxiety disorder.

patient.answer:
Well, let me think... it's been quite a while now. I'd say it really started about a year and two months ago. Yes, right around then. That's when we finally sold our house—the one we'd lived in for over thirty years, where we raised our daughter, you know? It was a beautiful place, a big colonial, but it was just getting to be too much upkeep for the two of us, especially with my husband's knees acting up, and the yard work was endless. 

So we decided to downsize and move into this condo. Which, at the time, seemed like the most sensible thing in the world. We found a lovely unit, great natural light, close to downtown... but almost the minute the ink was dry on the closing papers, this whole... cloud of worry just descended on me. 

I remember the first few nights in the new place, surrounded by all those boxes. I should have been relieved that the move was over, but instead, I was just lying awake, staring at an unfamiliar ceiling, second-guessing everything. Did we get enough for the house? Did we overpay for the condo? Are the neighbors going to be noisy? What if the building has structural issues they didn't disclose? And it just never stopped. It started with the move, about fourteen months ago, and instead of settling down once we got unpacked, the worrying just sort of... expanded. It latched onto the move first, and then it just kept finding new things to attach itself to, right up until today.

inference.note: The patient ruled out the possibility of obsessive-compulsive disorder (F40.00) as they do not endorse intrusive, ego-dystonic thoughts or compulsive behaviors typical of OCD. doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a major depressive episode, which would support a diagnosis of Major Depressive Disorder (F32) if present alongside other criteria.

patient.answer:
Well, no, not really. I mean, I wouldn't say I feel hopeless or down in the dumps like that. It's not a sadness, if that makes sense. It's more of a... a constant buzzing energy, but not the good kind of energy. It's that nervous, on-edge feeling, like I'm waiting for the other shoe to drop all the time. 

I certainly haven't lost interest in things. I still love my job, even though the market is just completely unpredictable right now—one minute houses are sitting for sixty days, and the next, there's a bidding war on a complete fixer-upper. I still enjoy taking my clients out, showing them properties, negotiating the deals. In fact, sometimes I think I throw myself into the work *too* much because it gives my brain something specific to focus on, even if I end up worrying about the contracts later. 

And I still love seeing my daughter, of course, and going out to dinner with my husband. We have this little Italian place we go to every Friday night, and I still look forward to that. We've been going there for fifteen years, they know exactly how I like my chicken piccata... So, no, I haven't lost interest in my life or felt hopeless for weeks on end. It’s just that I can’t seem to enjoy any of those things fully because there's always this underlying current of worry running through my mind while I'm doing them. I'm sitting there at dinner, eating my chicken, and part of my brain is wondering if I remembered to lock the patio door at the condo, or if the HOA is going to send out another special assessment notice. But no, no deep depression or hopelessness like you're describing. Just the worrying.

target_item.name: Excessive_Anxiety_Worry

patient.answer:
Well, yes. Yes, I do. That's exactly why I'm here, actually, because it feels like I worry about absolutely everything now, even when I'm just sitting on the sofa and nothing is technically wrong. It's just constant. I'll be sitting there, and suddenly I'm worrying about my clients, you know? Did I price that new listing correctly? Should we have painted the trim before putting it on the market? And then that spirals into worrying about the real estate market in general, because interest rates are doing whatever they're doing, and who knows if buyers are going to dry up completely by spring. 

And then, if it's not work, it's my family. I worry about my daughter, even though she's thirty-two and perfectly capable, but I'll wonder if she's saving enough for retirement or if she's working too many hours. And money—oh, I worry about money constantly, even though we made a good profit on the house. I just sit there and think, what if inflation eats away at our savings? What if my husband's knees get worse and he needs surgery and Medicare doesn't cover all the physical therapy?

I'll just be drinking my coffee, and my mind is racing through all these scenarios, and... and I know, logically, that it's out of proportion. I know I'm making mountains out of molehills, but I just can't seem to stop the wheels from turning. doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences symptoms of fatigue or low energy nearly every day, which would help distinguish between GAD (F41.1) and Adjustment Disorder with Anxiety (F43.22).

patient.answer:
Fatigued? You know, it's funny you ask that, because my husband, Richard, was just saying the other day that he doesn't know how I keep going at the pace I do. So, no, I wouldn't say I feel fatigued or low on energy at all. If anything, it's the exact opposite. Like I was saying before about that buzzing feeling? It's like I have too much energy, but it's all just... nervous energy. 

I'll be up at six in the morning, making coffee, pulling up the MLS listings on my iPad to see what went active overnight or what had a price drop, and from there I'm just... go, go, go. I'll run over to the condo association meeting—because let me tell you, if you don't stay on top of those people, they'll pass a special assessment for landscaping before you can even blink—and then I'm off showing houses all afternoon. 

But even when I haven't done anything taxing, like if I actually try to just sit down on a Sunday afternoon and watch a movie with Richard or read a book... I can't just sit there. My body might be resting, but my mind is running an absolute marathon, and I just end up getting up and reorganizing the hall closet or drafting emails to my clients for Monday morning. I'm just constantly revved up. Honestly, sometimes I wish I *could* feel a little fatigued, just so I could finally sit still for five minutes without feeling like I need to be doing something or checking on something. So, no, definitely no lack of energy here. Just the opposite, really.

patient.answer:
Well, yes, actually. That is something I’ve really been noticing lately, and it’s incredibly frustrating because, in my line of work, you absolutely cannot afford to miss a detail. Real estate is all about the details—the dates, the contingencies, the disclosures. But lately, with all this constant worrying I was telling you about, it’s like my brain just gets hijacked. 

For instance, just the other day I was sitting at my desk—well, my new desk at the condo, which I’m still trying to get organized because the lighting in that room is completely different from my old office—and I was trying to review a purchase agreement for my clients, the Millers. They’re buying this lovely mid-century modern place, but the inspection came back with some issues on the HVAC system, so I was drafting the inspection addendum. And I swear to you, I sat there and read the exact same paragraph three or four times. I’d start reading, and then suddenly I’m thinking, "Did I schedule the termite inspector for Tuesday or Wednesday?" or "What if the sellers completely reject this addendum and the whole deal falls apart and the Millers lose their earnest money?" 

And before I know it, I’m at the bottom of the page and I have absolutely no idea what I just read. My mind just goes completely blank on the task at hand because this other worry just barges in and takes over. I lose the thread entirely. I have to physically stop, take a breath, and force myself back to the top of the page. It’s exhausting, to be honest. I’ve always prided myself on being sharp and catching every little thing in these contracts, but now it takes me twice as long to get through a simple document because I just can't keep my focus where it needs to be. The worry just pulls me right out of it.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences symptoms of panic attacks, which would support a diagnosis of F41.1 (Panic Disorder) over F43.22 (Adjustment Disorder with Anxiety).
doctor.question: Have you ever experienced sudden episodes of intense fear or discomfort, where you felt like your heart was racing, you couldn't breathe, or you were losing control?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of panic attacks (sudden episodes of intense fear, racing heart, shortness of breath, feeling of losing control), which are not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No, I can't say I've ever had anything quite like that. Sudden episodes of intense fear? No, it's not like that at all. It's not a sudden spike or a panic, you know, where I feel like I'm losing control or can't breathe. I've heard of people having those—my sister-in-law, actually, had a terrible time with them after her divorce, said she felt like she was having a heart attack right in the middle of the grocery store by the produce section. But for me, it's never been like that. 

My heart doesn't suddenly start pounding out of my chest, and I don't get that suffocating feeling. It's more of a... well, like I was saying before, it's a constant, low-level hum of worry. It's always there, always churning in the background. It's not a sudden attack that comes out of nowhere and knocks me off my feet; it's just this steady stream of "what ifs" that I can't seem to turn off. Like, I'll be driving to a showing, and instead of just listening to the radio, I'm running through every possible thing that could go wrong with the appraisal, or wondering if I remembered to lock the back door at the condo, or worrying if Richard remembered to take his blood pressure medication. 

So, no, I wouldn't describe it as sudden or intense fear. I'm always very much in control, maybe too in control, honestly, because I'm trying to manage all these potential disasters in my head before they even happen. It's just exhausting because it never really peaks and goes away; it just stays with me all day long. But no, no racing heart or feeling like I can't breathe or anything like that. Just the constant, never-ending worry.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences symptoms of irritability related to their anxiety, which could support a diagnosis of Generalized Anxiety Disorder (F41.1).
doctor.question: Have you noticed yourself becoming more irritable or easily annoyed, especially when you're feeling overwhelmed by all the worrying?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about irritability, which is not listed in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Irritable? Oh, well... I mean, I suppose Richard might say so, but I don't really think I'm any more irritable than anyone else would be in my shoes. I mean, if you want to talk about being easily annoyed, you have to look at what I'm dealing with on a daily basis. 

Just yesterday, for example, I was trying to coordinate a final walk-through for a property over on Elm Street—a beautiful colonial, completely updated kitchen, but the sellers are just dragging their feet on moving their things out. And I'm sitting there, my mind is already spinning about whether the title company has the updated payoff statement, and whether the buyer's lender is going to clear the file to close on time, and then my phone rings. And it's the listing agent, telling me they need another day to get the garage cleaned out. 

Well, I just... I completely snapped at him. I told him that a contract is a contract and they can't just change the terms at the eleventh hour because they didn't plan their packing properly. And after I hung up, I did feel a little bad, because usually I'm very professional, very diplomatic. But it's like, when my brain is already juggling fifteen different "what ifs" and I'm so worried about everything falling apart, my patience is just... it's just nonexistent. 

And it happens with Richard, too, bless his heart. He'll ask me something simple, like what we should have for dinner, while I'm in the middle of worrying about an inspection report, and I'll just bite his head off. I'll say, "I can't possibly think about chicken versus fish right now, Richard, the entire plumbing system at the Oakwood house might need to be replaced!" So... I guess, yes, maybe I am a bit more irritable lately. But it's not like I'm just walking around angry for no reason. It's just that when I'm so overwhelmed by all the things that could go wrong, any little interruption or extra problem just feels like the straw that breaks the camel's back, you know? I just don't have the bandwidth for it.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the patient experiences symptoms of autonomic arousal (e.g., heart rate, sweating, trembling) during episodes of anxiety, which could help differentiate between GAD and adjustment disorder.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about autonomic physical symptoms of anxiety such as a fast heartbeat, sweating, or trembling, which are not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Sweating or trembling? No, not really. It’s kind of like what we were talking about earlier with the sudden panic—I just don't get those physical reactions. I mean, my mind will be going a million miles a minute, but my body doesn't really do all of that shaking or sweating. 

I actually had the perfect scenario for that just last Sunday, over in the Heritage subdivision. I was hosting an open house for this gorgeous four-bedroom craftsman. The sellers, lovely people, but they have three golden retrievers, so I had spent the entire morning just making sure there wasn't a single dog hair in sight, spraying linen mist, getting the lighting just right. And literally ten minutes before the open house is supposed to start, I realize the air conditioning isn't kicking on. It’s the middle of the afternoon, the sun is beating down on the big bay windows, and the thermostat is just climbing. 

Now, my mind immediately started spiraling. I’m thinking, "The buyers are going to walk in, they’re going to feel the heat, they’re going to assume the HVAC is completely shot, they’re going to think the house is a money pit, and this listing is going to sit on the market for months." I was worrying about having to explain to the sellers why we didn't get any offers, worrying about whether I should try to call an emergency repairman on a Sunday, which costs an absolute fortune. 

But even with all of that intense worry just flooding my brain, I wasn't physically shaking. My hands weren't trembling when I was setting out the sign-in sheets, and my heart wasn't racing. I mean, I might have been a little warm because the house was literally heating up, but I wasn't in a cold sweat or having nervous palpitations or anything like that. I was perfectly steady on the outside, greeting people at the door with a smile, handing out brochures. You would never look at me and think, "Oh, she's trembling," or "She looks shaky." It’s all entirely internal. It’s just that relentless mental churning, not my body actually shaking or my heart pounding out of my chest. So, no, I haven't really noticed any of those physical things you mentioned.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences difficulty controlling the worrying, which is a key feature of generalized anxiety disorder (F41.1) and helps differentiate it from adjustment disorder with anxiety (F43.22).

target_item.name: Uncontrollable_Worry

patient.answer:
Oh, absolutely. It’s... it’s exactly like that. It’s like a runaway train, honestly. I know in my logical brain—I have a degree, I’ve been in this business for decades, I know how these transactions work—I know that most of what I’m worrying about isn’t going to happen, or at least, it’s not life-or-death. But stopping it? That’s an entirely different story. 

Just the other night, for instance, it was maybe 9:30 or 10:00, Richard was already asleep, and I was just doing a quick check of my emails on my iPad before turning out the light. And there was a message from a buyer's agent on a beautiful little townhome I have listed over in the new development on Pine Street. Just a simple question, really, asking if the seller would be willing to leave the custom drapes in the dining room. Now, normally, that’s a five-minute conversation for the next business day. No big deal. 

I literally said out loud to the empty room, I said, "Parin, this is not urgent." I told myself to just put it away. I closed the iPad, I turned off the lamp, and I laid my head on the pillow. But then I’m lying there in the dark, and my brain just starts going. I start thinking, well, if they want the drapes, maybe they’re going to be nitpicky about the inspection items. And if they’re difficult about the inspection, what if they ask for a credit for that tiny, old water stain in the guest bath? And if they ask for a credit, my sellers might get offended and want to kill the deal. And suddenly, I’m worrying about the house going back on the market, and the days on market ticking up, and having to explain to the sellers why we lost the buyer... 

It’s just... one concern leads to another, you know? It's a complete domino effect in my head. And before I know it, I’ve spent half an hour just lying there replaying small details I meant to let go of. I’ll go over every single word in that short email, wondering if the agent's tone was aggressive, or if I should have just negotiated the drapes in the initial contract. It’s completely irrational, I know it is! I know I need to sleep. But I just can't seem to put the brakes on it once it starts. I just can't turn the worry off.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences symptoms of fatigue or low energy in line with a major depressive episode, which would support F43.22 (Adjustment Disorder with Mixed Anxiety and Depressed Mood) over F41.1 (Generalized Anxiety Disorder).

Fatigued for no reason? Oh, heavens, no. No, if anything, I think I have the exact opposite problem. I mean, my mind is always going so fast that it just pulls my body right along with it. If I'm tired, there is always a very, very clear reason for it. I certainly don't just sit around feeling drained out of nowhere. 

Just to give you an idea of what my schedule is like, let me tell you about my Thursday. I was up at 5:30 in the morning because I had to meet a staging company at this gorgeous mid-century modern over on Maple Drive—prime location, absolutely stunning original hardwood floors, but the sellers had completely moved out, so it was just an empty box. And I get there, and the stagers are unloading the truck, and I realize they’ve brought this dreadful, cool-toned gray sectional for the living room, which completely clashed with the warm teak paneling on the accent wall. I mean, it was a disaster waiting to happen. Buyers are so visual, they would have walked in and just felt like the room was cold, you know? 

So, I spent the next three hours personally driving back and forth to their warehouse across town to help them pick out a beautiful cognac leather sofa instead. And then I had two back-to-back showings in the afternoon, plus a final walk-through where the buyer threw an absolute fit because a lightbulb was burnt out in the half-bath—which I ended up changing myself, by the way, in a pencil skirt and heels—and then I didn't get home to Richard until almost 8:00 PM. 

So, when I finally sat down on the couch and felt tired, well, I had certainly earned it! It wasn't just some mysterious loss of energy. I was exhausted because I had been running on pure adrenaline and espresso for fourteen hours straight. So, no, I really can't say I ever just feel fatigued for no reason. I’m always on the go, always doing something, and honestly, even when I *want* to feel tired and just relax, my brain is usually still buzzing too much to let me.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences difficulty falling or staying asleep due to anxiety, which would help differentiate between GAD (F41.1) and Adjustment Disorder with Anxiety (F43.22).
doctor.question: Do you often have trouble falling asleep or staying asleep, even when you’re not actively thinking about something specific?

target_item.name: Sleep_Disturbance
target_item.manifestation: Most nights I get into bed at a reasonable hour, but my mind keeps circling through condo fees, tomorrow’s showings, and whether I missed something in a contract, so it takes me a long time to settle and I wake up feeling like I never fully rested.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about trouble falling or staying asleep, which corresponds directly to the Sleep Disturbance symptom.

patient.answer:
Well, see, that's the trick of it—I am almost *always* actively thinking about something specific. I really do try my best to have good habits. Most nights I get into bed at a perfectly reasonable hour, usually right after I put the iPad away like I mentioned earlier. I want to be asleep by ten because my mornings are just so demanding in this business. 

But my mind just refuses to cooperate. It just keeps circling and circling through all the minutiae of the day. I’ll be lying there in the quiet, and suddenly I’m going over condo fees for a new listing, trying to remember if the special assessment for the roof was already paid out by the seller or if the buyer has to assume it. And then, before I know it, I’m mentally mapping out tomorrow’s showings, worrying if I left enough buffer time for traffic between the west side properties and the suburbs. And then I'll start second-guessing myself, just agonizing over whether I missed something in a contract I submitted that afternoon—did I check the right box for the appraisal contingency? Did I get all the required initials on the lead paint disclosure? 

It takes me such a terribly long time to finally settle down and drift off because I'm just reviewing all these files in my head, over and over. And because of all that mental gymnastics, when the alarm finally does go off, I wake up feeling like I never fully rested at all. It's like my brain was working the night shift while I was supposed to be sleeping, so I just start the next day feeling completely unrefreshed.

inference.note: The patient continues to exhibit persistent and excessive worry across multiple domains, difficulty controlling the worry, and associated symptoms such as trouble falling asleep and trouble concentrating. There is no evidence of panic attacks, significant mood symptoms, or fatigue/lack of energy, which maintains the differential between Generalized Anxiety Disorder (F41.1) and Adjustment Disorder with Anxiety (F43.22). No new information has ruled out either diagnosis.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences excessive anxiety specifically about physical symptoms or health concerns, which would be more indicative of a somatic symptom disorder or another anxiety-related condition, and would help distinguish between GAD (F41.1) and Adjustment Disorder with Anxiety (F43.22).
doctor.question: Have you ever found yourself excessively worried about your physical health or specific bodily symptoms, even when doctors have told you there’s no serious issue?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about excessive worry regarding physical health or bodily symptoms (health anxiety/illness anxiety), which is not covered by the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Oh, no, not at all. My health is probably the one thing I *don't* obsess over. Honestly, I just don't have the time to sit around wondering about every little ache and pain! If something hurts, I usually know exactly why it hurts, and it's almost always related to my schedule. 

Like, just last month, I had this terrible, shooting pain in my lower back, just radiating down my left leg. Richard was practically hovering over me, telling me I needed to go to a specialist, worrying it could be a slipped disc or some kind of permanent nerve damage or something awful. But I told him, I said, "Richard, I have been walking up and down three flights of stairs at those new luxury builds on Elm Street for three days straight, and I’ve been doing it in two-inch heels because the developer was on-site and I needed to look sharp." I didn't think for a second it was some mysterious, life-threatening disease. I just knew it was the stairs and the shoes!

I did end up going to my regular doctor, Dr. Aris, mostly just to get Richard to stop nagging me about it. And Dr. Aris did a quick exam and said it was just a bit of mild sciatica from overuse, told me to take some ibuprofen and maybe switch to flats for a few days. Which, by the way, is practically impossible in high-end real estate if you want to maintain a certain level of professionalism, but I digress. 

The point is, when he told me it was nothing serious, I completely believed him. I was just relieved I didn't have to take time off! I didn't go home and look up symptoms on the internet or demand an MRI or worry that he missed something. I just went to the department store, bought a pair of sensible wedges with decent arch support, and went right back to work. So, no, I don't really worry about my body failing me or anything like that. It’s the escrows and the appraisals that give me gray hair, not my health!

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences excessive anxiety specifically about separation or being alone, which would help differentiate between GAD (F41.1) and Adjustment Disorder with Anxiety (F43.22)
doctor.question: Do you ever feel particularly anxious or distressed when you're away from family members or worried about something bad happening to them when you're not around?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of separation anxiety (anxiety when away from family members or fear of something bad happening to them when separated), which is not covered by my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Oh, no, not really. I mean, Richard and I have been married for thirty-four years, and our daughter, Chloe, she's thirty-two now and lives in Chicago, so we're all very independent people. I certainly don't sit around worrying that something terrible is going to happen to them just because I'm not in the room. 

In fact, just last week, Richard went on this fishing trip with his brother up to a lake in Michigan. They go every year, and they are completely off the grid for four days. No cell service, no Wi-Fi, nothing. And honestly, it is wonderful! I don't mean that in a bad way, of course I love him, but having the house to myself for a few days? It's glorious. I can spread out all my listing paperwork on the dining room table without him complaining about the mess, I can watch my home renovation shows on HGTV without him making sarcastic comments about the open-concept floor plans, and I can just focus entirely on my clients. 

I didn't spend one single second of those four days worrying that his boat had capsized or that he'd been eaten by a bear or whatever else could happen in the woods. I knew he was with his brother, they know what they're doing, and I had three open houses to prep for that weekend anyway. I was far more concerned about whether the caterer was going to deliver the artisan cheese platters on time for the Sunday showing at the new subdivision than I was about Richard's fishing trip. 

And it's the same with Chloe. She travels all the time for her consulting job—she's always flying off to Denver or Seattle or New York. And she's a smart girl, she knows how to handle herself in an airport and navigate a new city. I don't feel the need to track her flights or text her every five minutes to make sure she made it to her hotel safely. We'll catch up on Sunday evenings, she'll tell me about her week, I'll tell her about the absolute nightmare I had trying to negotiate a seller down on a property that needed a new HVAC system, and that's that. So, no, I don't have that kind of anxiety about being apart from my family at all. My worries are almost entirely reserved for my real estate transactions, I assure you!

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences excessive anxiety specifically about work responsibilities, which would support GAD.
doctor.question: Do you find that your worries are often focused on your work performance or responsibilities, even when there’s no immediate problem?

target_item.name: Excessive_Anxiety_Worry
target_item.manifestation: I came in because I seem to worry about everything now—clients, the market, my family, money, even whether moving to the condo was the right decision—and it feels out of proportion to what is actually happening.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the specific domains of my worry (work performance and responsibilities) and its excessive nature (even when there's no immediate problem), which maps to excessive anxiety and worry about various events or activities.

patient.answer:
Well, yes, work is a huge part of it, like I was just saying about the contracts and the escrows. But honestly, doctor, that's exactly why I finally made this appointment. It’s not just work anymore. I came in because I seem to worry about absolutely everything now. I mean, it just never stops. 

Yes, it’s my clients, and it’s the housing market—which, with the way interest rates are fluctuating right now, you can imagine the stress, it's enough to give anyone an ulcer—but it bleeds into everything else. It's money, it's my family... and I know I just said I don't panic when Richard goes off the grid or when Chloe travels, but I do worry about them in other ways, constantly. Are they saving enough for retirement? Is Chloe working too many hours? 

And then there are these big life choices that just consume my thoughts. Like, we recently downsized, and I spend hours just agonizing over whether moving to the condo was the right decision. I'll sit there at the kitchen island, looking at the quartz countertops, and just fret about whether we rushed into it, or if the HOA board is going to mismanage the reserve funds, or if we should have kept the larger house just in case. 

And the frustrating thing is, I know it doesn't make sense. I step back and look at all of this—the clients, the market, the family, the money, the condo—and it just feels completely out of proportion to what is actually happening. There's almost never an immediate problem! The condo is lovely, the market always ebbs and flows, everyone is fine... but my brain just treats every single little thing like an absolute crisis, and I just can't seem to turn the volume down on it.

opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with persistent and excessive worry across multiple domains (work, family, finances, housing), difficulty controlling the worry, associated sleep disturbance, irritability, and concentration difficulties, all of which have been present for over a year and cause significant functional impairment. These symptoms align with generalized anxiety disorder (GAD). Adjustment disorder with anxiety (F43.22) was considered but ruled out due to the chronicity, pervasiveness, and severity of the anxiety beyond what would be expected in response to a specific stressor.
